In mathematics, '''Milnor maps''' are named in honor of [[John Milnor]], who introduced them to [[topology]] and [[algebraic geometry]] in his book '''''Singular Points of Complex Hypersurfaces''''' ([[Princeton University Press]], 1968) and earlier lectures. The most studied Milnor maps are actually [[fibration]]s, and the phrase '''Milnor fibration''' is more commonly encountered in the mathematical literature. These were introduced to study isolated singularities by constructing numerical [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariants]] related to the topology of a smooth [[Deformation (mathematics)|deformation]] of the singular space.

== Definition ==
Let <math>f(z_0,\dots,z_n)</math> be a non-constant [[polynomial function]] of <math>n+1</math> [[Complex analysis|complex variables]] <math>z_0,\dots,z_n</math> where the vanishing locus of
:<math>f(z)\ \text{ and }\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z_i}(z)</math>
is only at the origin, meaning the associated [[Algebraic variety|variety]] <math>X = V(f)</math> is not [[Smooth variety|smooth]] at the origin. Then, for <math>K = X \cap S^{2n+1}_{\varepsilon}</math> (a sphere inside <math>\mathbb{C}^{n+1}</math> of radius <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>) the '''Milnor fibration'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Dimca|first= Alexandru|author-link=Alexandru Dimca|title=Singularities and Topology of Hypersurfaces|date=1992|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|isbn=978-1-4612-4404-2|location=New York, NY|oclc=852790417}}</ref><sup>pg 68</sup> associated to <math>f</math> is defined as the map
:<math>\phi\colon (S_\varepsilon^{2n+1}\setminus K) \to S^1\ \text{ sending } \ x \mapsto \frac{f(x)}{|f(x)|}</math>,
which is a locally trivial [[Smooth map|smooth]] [[fibration]] for sufficiently small <math>\varepsilon</math>. Originally this was proven as a theorem by Milnor, but was later taken as the definition of a Milnor fibration. Note this is a well defined map since
:<math>f(x) = |f(x)|\cdot e^{2\pi i \operatorname{Arg}(f(x))}</math>,
where <math>\operatorname{Arg}(f(x))</math> is the [[Argument (complex analysis)|argument of a complex number]].

=== Historical motivation ===
One of the original motivations for studying such maps was in the study of [[Knot theory|knots]] constructed by taking an <math>\varepsilon</math>-ball around a singular point of a [[plane curve]], which is isomorphic to a real 4-dimensional ball, and looking at the knot inside the boundary, which is a 1-[[manifold]] inside of a 3-[[sphere]]. Since this concept could be generalized to [[Complex hypersurface|hypersurfaces]] with isolated singularities, Milnor introduced the subject and proved his theorem.

=== In algebraic geometry ===
Another closed related notion in [[algebraic geometry]] is the Milnor fiber of an isolated hypersurface singularity. This has a similar setup, where a polynomial <math>f</math> with <math>f = 0</math> having a singularity at the origin, but now the polynomial
:<math>f_t\colon \mathbb{C}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{C}\ \text{ sending }\ (z_0,\ldots,z_n)\mapsto f(z_0,\ldots,z_n) - t</math>
is considered. Then, the '''algebraic Milnor fiber''' is taken as one of the polynomials <math>f_{t\neq 0}</math>.

== Properties and Theorems ==

=== Parallelizability ===
One of the basic structure theorems about Milnor fibers is they are [[parallelizable manifold]]s<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 75</sup>.

=== Homotopy type ===
Milnor fibers are special because they have the [[homotopy type]] of a [[bouquet of spheres]]<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 78</sup>. The number of these spheres is the [[Milnor number]]. In fact, the number of spheres can be computed using the formula
:<math>\mu(f) = \text{dim}_\mathbb{C}\frac{\mathbb{C}[[z_0,\ldots,z_n]]}{\operatorname{Jac}(f)},</math>
where the quotient ideal is the [[Jacobian ideal]], defined by the partial derivatives <math>\partial f / \partial z_i</math>. These spheres deformed to the algebraic Milnor fiber are the [[Vanishing cycle|Vanishing cycles]] of the fibration<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 83</sup>. Computing the eigenvalues of their monodromy is computationally challenging and requires advanced techniques such as [[B-function|b-functions]]<ref>{{Cite web|last=Budur|first=Nero|date=|title=Multiplier ideals, Milnor fibers, and other singularity invariants| url=http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/d683/1f275409bb35b5704619bebe7b20a784ef16.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306225030/http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/d683/1f275409bb35b5704619bebe7b20a784ef16.pdf|archive-date=6 March 2019|access-date=|website=|doi=10.1002/humu.22655 |s2cid=221776902 }}</ref><sup>pg 23</sup>.

=== Milnor's fibration theorem ===
Milnor's Fibration Theorem states that, for every <math>f</math> such that the origin is a [[Singular point of a curve|singular point]] of the hypersurface <math>V_f</math> (in particular, for every non-constant [[square-free polynomial]] <math>f</math> of two variables, the case of plane curves), then for <math>\epsilon</math> sufficiently small,

:<math>\dfrac{f}{|f|}\colon \left(S^{2n+1}_{\varepsilon} \setminus V_f \right) \to S^1</math>

is a fibration.  Each fiber is a non-compact [[differentiable manifold]] of real dimension <math>2n</math>. Note that the closure of each fiber is a compact [[manifold]] with boundary. Here the boundary corresponds to the intersection of <math>V_f</math> with the <math>(2n+1)</math>-sphere (of sufficiently small radius) and therefore it  is a real manifold of dimension <math>(2n-1)</math>.  Furthermore, this compact manifold with boundary, which is known as the ''Milnor fiber'' (of the isolated singular point of <math>V_f</math> at the origin), is diffeomorphic to the intersection of the closed <math>(2n+2)</math>-ball (bounded by the small <math>(2n+1)</math>-sphere) with the (non-singular) hypersurface <math>V_g</math> where <math>g=f-e</math> and <math>e</math> is any sufficiently small non-zero [[complex number]].  This small piece of hypersurface is also called  a ''Milnor fiber''.

Milnor maps at other radii are not always fibrations, but they still have many interesting properties.  For most (but not all) polynomials, the '''Milnor map at infinity''' (that is, at any sufficiently large radius) is again a fibration.

== Examples ==
The Milnor map of <math>f(z,w)=z^2+w^3</math> at any radius is a fibration; this construction gives the [[trefoil knot]] its structure as a [[fibered knot]].
